Back in 2015, when I was still at Google, there was a small group of code-golf enthusiasts spending hours trying to save just one byte on their solutions for weekly code-golf problems. No matter how hard you tried, there always seemed to be another Googler who found a shorter solution. And once a problem entered the challenge phase and every solution became public, it was always astonishing to read how brilliant other people's solutions were.

11 years later, LLMs are evolving fast. A recent OpenAI post ("Perplexity and Intelligence", https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/) described researchers watching a model solve open math problems one after another in a Slack thread. I started to wonder: how would frontier models compete with the records that a small group of brilliant minds created with hours of effort each week?

So I built this benchmark. Frontier models do find a lot of new approaches (and very brilliant ones) to solve these problems. For example, in two problems ("Surviving Queens" and "The Rolling Dice"), frontier models use complex numbers to solve them in Python and Ruby (both languages have built-in complex number support). And for the "(-5)-Smooth Numbers" problem, where you have to write code to list the first n positive integers of the form (-2)^x⋅(-3)^y⋅(-5)^z, most solutions build them with nested loops or by growing a set, then sort. GPT-6.2 Astra gets them all from powers of 4, and earns a sole best with this brilliant solution:

    g=lambda n:sorted(4**i%(2**999-5)%(2**49-3)for i in range(7000))[:n]
There is a dedicated section for this: https://bjin.github.io/go-codegolf-benchmark/#why/finding-a-...

It's nice to see GPT-6.2 Astra become the first frontier model to beat the human records in code golfing. Along with other frontier models, it finds a lot of interesting solutions that Googlers back in 2015 didn't. On the other hand, I also believe code golfing can be a good benchmark (not a comprehensive one, of course) for frontier models.

Code golfing rewards thinking differently, because a shorter solution usually comes from looking at the problem from a different angle. It also rewards running experiments, not just thinking: writing a search program to find a shorter expression, or exploring lesser-known features and functions in the target compiler, interpreter, or library. Human code golfers do this a lot, and no public training data tells a frontier model how to do so.

We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

Hi all, I am a professor in algorithm engineering. In our field we use a method of falsifiable hypothesis testing to improve algorithms. More precisely, this is a cycle consisting of designing an algorithm, analyzing the algorithm, then implementing it and lastly testing it using experiments on real-world instances which leads to designing new algorithms based on the current observations.

We put this methodology into an AI skill which runs in an infinite loop. This skill first creates a performance profile, then produces a hypothesis which is implemented and tested automatically using an AI agent. If the change improved the performance and tests negotiated with the user verify it, the change is kept, if not it is discarded. Everything is tracked via version control.

Part of the output is a pdf report which documents all the code changes and progress over time as well as individual patches to only merge specific patches if one chooses to do so. Moreover, this comes with a knowledge-base in which we collect global optimization knowledge, thereby improving the skill over time.

We ran this on a wide range of public code bases, e.g. our KaHIP graph partitioning toolkit, which improved running time by 3.9x, or our VieCut minimum cut solver, where the skill improved the running time of the system by 8.9x; I do believe the skill is very easy to use and hence am sharing this here. Let me know what you think!

RCHIVE is a cross-platform desktop app for cataloging, searching and reorganizing files on your computers and drives. Like, all of 'em: internal, external, network shares, USB sticks, loose SD cards, weird CD-R's, DVDs, floppy disks, Zip disks, and everything in between.

I built this thing because my digital archives are an embarrassment! 30 years of getting a new hard drive whenever capacity quadrupled and dragging the old one to it into a folder titled "BACKUP - TO SORT" will do that to you lol, especially when you know deep down that "sorting" will never happen. To try to deal with that growing mess on a daily basis, I've tried a patchwork of all of our favorites in the past -- Everything, grep, custom scripts, you name it. And don't get me started on built-in OS defaults like Windows Explorer, Finder, Spotlight. I figured it was time to make something better-suited to my tastes, and 4200 commits later here we are!

RCHIVE scans as many different sources as you throw at it, gives you unified deep search across the entire catalog (with drives connected or disconnected), allows you to virtually organize and clean up giant archives of digital stuff by applying recipes and transformations, resiliently copies or moves files when you're ready to actually restructure on disk, or just lets you quickly pop in to find something or browse everything with previews, metadata, etc.

It works on Windows, Mac or Linux, works offline, has zero telemetry, deletes nothing, and is fully deterministic in operation. So, no wacky AI integrations for decision making or classification, everything is predictable and repeatable, you can even run portable versions off of a USB drive if you don't want to install it.

I've been using it all day every day for a year and am just stoked to have it out there, get some users, get some feedback (good or bad), and see what people think. There's a free trial, no email address or anything needed.

The website is also full of videos, features, comparisons, all that stuff, as well as a ncdu-like companion app for figuring out where the hell all your disk space went.

Anyways, check it out! Should come in handy if you're ever in Grand Central trying to find a garbage file left on some dude's Gibson.

https://www.rchive.computer

Ribbon Architect is available as a free iOS app and in the browser.

Scan or measure a gift, browse pattern suggestions made for its exact proportions, or construct your own designs. Then step-by-step instructions show you how to lay the ribbon on your gift.

Gifts are modeled as convex polyhedra, so many non-cuboid gift shapes, such as prisms, work too and have their own interesting ribbon patterns.

A ribbon (without twists) that is pulled tight follows a locally shortest path, a geodesic. This is a path on the surface of the gift that runs straight on faces and folds correctly over edges and loops back on itself. As you'll see in the app, geodesics can be much more interesting than the axis-aligned loops that people usually tie when wrapping a gift.

Click "Browse geodesics" on the first screen of the app, to get a glimpse of the endless variety of geodesics. (It currently stops after 5'000 or earlier depending on available memory. In theory, a box has infinitely many distinct geodesics.)

For further variety, you can combine these building blocks by inserting twists: When twisted, two strands of ribbon that follow sections of geodesics that cross, turn over and follow the other geodesic. This can join two geodesics into a single ribbon. Click any crossing to insert a twist (after selecting a pattern or after drawing ribbons in "draw your own" mode). Or follow the tutorial (the ? icon in the upper right corner).

This is the first version. The browser version hasn't been tested on many browsers and devices. Please let me know if you run into any issues.

Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres.

So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up. But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres. Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads.

So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres.

We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone:

- pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them)

- pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both)

- materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads)

- firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers)

- redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic)

And we shortlisted 3:

- pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse)

- cedarDB (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database)

- duckdb (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect)

We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases. We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment.

We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results:

- pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time).

- cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time).

- duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time).

Matched meant they returned exactly the same result as postgres. Refused meant they returned an error message (usually telling you some syntax isn’t recognised). And “wrong” meant they didn’t return the same results as postgres. I appreciate that arguably postgres may be the one that is wrong in some cases - but for our use case, we considered postgres the golden source of truth.

So, both duckdb and cedardb performed pretty well (correctly handled more than 80% of the postgres queries we threw at it), out-of-the box. But we really still wanted to try and cover that long-tail.

We chose duckdb as its open-source license would allow us to easily work on the long tail to get the postgres SQL parity we wanted.

So, Mason (linked above), is what we built, powered by duckdb, which now matches postgres on 96% of our 5,410 queries, plus hundreds of other queries that we added, testing it with Metabase, Grafana, Superset, DBeaver and Trevor.io. For the remaining 4%, it errors with a nice clear message telling you how to rewrite your SQL.

We’d love your feedback on what we’ve built. Useful? How can we make it better?

I created joonoo.art to turn family photos into picture books and comics. I was inspired to do it last summer because my granddaughter was very enthusiastic when I made up stories with her as the hero.

It's been a major struggle to get it working consistently, though. It's hard enough to have ONE character be consistent in a series of images you create using image generation models like nano banana, but to maintain consistency of up to 4 main characters, all the side characters, the props (like dragons, submarines, spaceships, or what have you) throughout the book is a Herculean struggle! On top of that, I got really ambitious and wanted to do a worldwide launch supporting 24 languages - you can imagine the amount of testing it takes! It really buried me - especially as a side project.

I nearly gave up on it. After I launched last year, I got a few orders and the customers who got the books (primarily in English in the U.S.) were happy, but I did not feel comfortable publicizing the product, so it languished. But then Fable came along and gave me hope. After a few months working with the great capabilities of Fable and Claude Code, I was able to relaunch - this time in fewer languages and countries.

As the public starts to use it, they are stretching the limits of what's possible, so it's a constant struggle, but it's also a great learning and hardening experience! To others struggling with similar quests, I would strongly recommend the superpowers framework for Claude Code - and building in the testing is the most important thing you could do to succeed. I would also love to hear if you have any advice for me.

The website itself was created using the impeccable plugin and Google fonts - and design and consumer-friendliness was paramount. I am very pleased with it, and customers have said that they love it. There are tons of examples - mostly AI-generated family photos and the comics and picture books created using those photos.

For example, https://joonoo.art/books/mystery-of-the-lighthouse-key/read shows you a photo of 3 siblings and the full comic book that was created using that photo.

You can find tons more example books and comics to scroll through in video form here: https://joonoo.art/videos. If you'd rather scroll through the pages, start here: https://joonoo.art/comics or here: https://joonoo.art/picture-books

I am very eager to hear from you!

I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code.

What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me.

I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins.

I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great.

Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...).

Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.

Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine (https://versine.com). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon.

Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like:

- Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app)

- Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once

- Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins)

- Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this)

Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0

We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer.

Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as

1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP.

Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval.

Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns.

Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds.

Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address.

Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake.

We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP).

Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot.

We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents.

Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!

https://versine.com

Hey HN! I'm Lakshay, and at Cerulion we cooked up a harness for physical AI. Built on top of our deterministic runtime, we now have MCP tools that let any LLM see and move a robot. It closes the loop with measurements so a model doesn't try to guess its way through the task, and imbues common sense and robotics best practices into the workflow.

We ran the numbers on LIBERO-PRO and quite frankly are a bit shocked. Gemini 3.8 Flash with Cerulion solved 73 of 100 LIBERO-PRO tasks. GPT-6 Astra on a bare 3-tool baseline (arXiv:2610.30051) solved 71, at about 12x the cost and 3x the wall time per run. Flash on that same baseline solved 25.

Guys. Gemini 3.8 Flash matched GPT-6 Astra for robotics. Model intelligence is not the bottleneck. A harness is all you need ;)

Star us and follow along. Try the quickstart, lmk what you guys wanna see next. I'll post again soon! (teaser: my Nespresso machine is getting a lot of attention from my robot arm)

There have been questions about why the /ask page (https://news.ycombinator.com/ask) was running dry of Ask HNs - e.g.:

Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments)

Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments)

I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.

p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.
